title: Are people building AI game studios?
author: TheUniverseOrNothing
selftext:
Look at all the results we are seeing from solo devs. Is it pointless to invest in say an office in Reno and have 10 MAC mini’s setup and a small team working on games using Claude Code and Codex?

I know it’s more nuanced and not black and white. But I’m at the point where I could really use some extra help and want to develop things with a team.

I’ve been running a marketing business for 10 years and have a solid network of people I work with in that sector and many real devs I outsource to when I need certain builds.

But I really am tempted to move to Nevada where there is no income tax and move my marketing business while also focusing on creating solid things with AI.

replies.author: EasyTarget973
replies.body:
Sure. At the current pace, the level of content available will just define it (supply, demand). Game Companies were already in trouble before this explosion of ai-driven game development. Not all game companies, obviously this industry makes a ton of money, but the incoming shift -> will limit risk, and game companies require tons of cash to start up (currently). Put yourself in the shoes of the studios, SO many will just be shutting down because there's no viable way to become profitable. 

There will still be some probably MASSIVE games out there you pay for, and maybe instead of free games are incredibly cheap. I've been a game dev for 20 years, which doesn't make my take correct at all, I've just been thinking about it quite a bit lol. There are a lot of variables.

Expect that the people do hobby projects they find out they cannot make money from it and give up. You have a surge in the webpages and games and after it is gone.

Making one prompt game or pre ai quality with AI is not means it will be able to compete with studio made games. 

I have 10+ years experience in game dev and 15 years in total as software engineer. The bottleneck on iteration and tech debt is basically gone, I just see somewhere tech debt I can just fix it on side and on other side implementing other 3 features and I take on designing features too. This is a single person in the studio! 

I think quality and fun factor of games will skyrocket, where there is investment.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
Honestly... while it is a fool's errand to predict the future, I think some set-up like this really will become how the games industry operates in the future. Horizontal production rather than vertical - a bunch of people in a building with a few computers and a shared cloud account and a dream, or just wanting to punch in a shift and put in an honest day's work for someone else's dream.

IF - and it is a very big if, but - IF 10 guys in a little office in Reno can make something the equivalent of even just a really solid AAA game at a fraction of the cost and time, because of the advantages of horizontal production... that could be a thing that would kick off another golden age of video game development. Suddenly it's not a rigid hierarchy of skilled developers with QA below them, it's a mix of people from all walks of life using their native language to build something as part of a production line.

If successful, that would be completely wild and utterly, forever, change how people look at software development (again, huge IF there. IF pulling so much weight here it makes Atlas blush).

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
The AAA studios use AI too 10 people will never out produce AAA, AAA just means the production cost, not how the game is developed.

Now in AI era, many studios have automated bug fixing pipelines and one person works multiple features simultaneously. The bottleneck is literally the workstation and build times + finding the fun in game and iteration and to make sure the insane amount of out put is manageable in long run. Creative and architectural choices are what you make when the AI is implementing. 

I personally always work on 4 different features in panellise my work.

This not means 10 people cannot make a great game, it just means they cannot make same big game as AAA studios who were be able to make great games before AI will make great games who weren’t they will not.

There are AAA quality games which were not made by AAA studios before too(Hellblade for example).

replies.author: Mother-Hedgehog-5628
replies.body: This is not true at all, the problem with bigger companies and studios isnt how quickly they can make stuff its how many layers decisions have to go through for things to have traction - yes they will be faster with AI, but they wont be as agile as as much smaller team or solo dev, and the solo dev can experiment completely free form to come up with crazy stuff that tripple A wouldnt even bother looking into... using programming as an example, people have always been able to build insane things full of features, but minimum viable product usually wins out historically with how long changes took and related testing. now with AI its very easy to prototype anything from a single prompt and then dial it in with a few more words and fully automated regression testing...  obviously not exactly that easy but my point is its never been easier to try new stuff - it really confuses me why people spend so much time cloning existing games and porting things into another game... when the idea used to be the "easy" part, executing it was the time consuming part and thats almost flipping now with AI.... people just need to focus more on the design and UX....    sorry for wall of text... couldn't stop adding side thoughts....

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
I think I would agree with you here, and this is why I think we will see a dot com style turnover of companies. People are trying to bolt AI into existing structures when really AI is a whole new paradigm which needs new structures.

What would have taken a team of mixed skills at least a month to build can now be done in a day or two by a couple of people. I’m not talking finished games but prototypes, MVPs and other tools to prove something works. When you get rid of the huge cost of experimentation you open up a very different way of working.

replies.author: Count_JohnnyJ
replies.body: I started by cloning old games into modern remakes. I did it for a couple of reasons: 1. I wanted to have a modern remake of the game. 2. The original game functioned like a project map for me, and I was able to tackle one piece at a time to learn how to effectively get what I want out of the AI without also having to learn how to be a real project manager from scratch. Once I had a firm grasp on how to use the AI tools effectively, I started my own unique project and learned the project management stuff in the second round.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
I think the first assumption misses the point here. Many AAA studios use small cross-discipline teams, to work on features. I work at studio with million+ players and we have 3-6 sized cross discipline teams, we have design direction based on target audience, but the designers plan the game without really any limitations.

Even studios like dice have smaller teams, cross-discipline teams.

The programming is great example for this, people could build crazy stuff before, but it was way less value for players, then expensive. Now because the expenses went down, the value of those things against the cost is going up.

That you can do more, it not means you will just throw insane amounts of features in game it means you are able to deliver way higher quality and detail to feature.  
Or you can make way more immersive games. 

Silly example, pour coffee in cup and let character walk around with it and let it spill out when the character does some quick movement. Well, this feature would be super expensive maybe used in one place in game and it would be high cost to do. Now it is cheap so you can add it and other one hundred things like this. If you add many of these immersive features, you will get a really immersive experience at the end. 

I think those games will win which can add more background features and more immersion to their game. Look at gta they are doing exactly this.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
My suggestion is to interview one of those game devs (a capable programmer) and ask them about hardware, because with Mac mini, the bottleneck can be the computer.

Some more insights about the roles(this is by my personal experience), I guess you have experience in hiring, but I will say this anyway. I would suggest to use agency who specialise in hiring game devs. I seen many projects die, because they seen a fancy resume and they hired the wrong person. So about the roles:  
\- Designer/UX designer - These guys, will make your game awesome(which type of designer you need) is really depends on what game you want to do. In general the design will be your bottleneck. Million small decisions to maximise the player experience.  
\- Game programmer - I know you could vibe code the game, but a game programmer is more efficient and can take responsibility for the code. If you want to make bigger project I would suggest to have at least some programmers. People who are just vibe coders are useless, what they can do a designer can do and the designer will make your game better too. The programmer is important too to setup proper harness.  
\- 2d/3d artists - Even if you want to go full AI most of the artists who I know are extremely efficient in setting up pipelines and doing fast iterations, they are many times better in it then the programmers. You want to shit out 100 game assets, search for artist who can do art and let them setup the art pipeline, they can make your game look awesome.

This is only based on my personal experience! 

Now I probably, do not need to mention that be super straightforward about that your company is focused on ai supported development.

I would suggest to start with extremely small team, who can lye the foundation. 

If you pick up a clever unicorn as programmer or designer or mix of too. Your game will become awesome.

Another thing, you will work with creative people, let them be creative and assume they are better game developers than you. (I do this always I assume people who I work with it are smarter or know more than me, so when I evaluate the design or technical aspects I try to look into it from their side.)

I used to make music myself, I was very talented at writing, understanding music and deconstructing its influence and notes and stuff.

Now, that music has been brought down to 0 entry level. It is even more ahead than Video Games. You can literally AI generate any song you want by humming it and pick styles and instruments, or even do less, simply generate a song and give it your voice to insert.

That being said, the best artists are the ones with the best vision, sure some songs will trend that are fully generated without input, but I think the ones where the person makes it quirkier will go through, and the ones that are well thought out. 

Some people may be more influencer types in the future, some attractive gen z guy who puts his games out and people play cause they like the influencer, just like in music, many tiktokers put out AI slop music and they get on the charts, 

but also some will have a good story, and will be well thought out with AI assistance. 

Others will just be copies with full ai used, and they may strike at gold.

Big studios WILL struggle, and many will shut down, especially ones that make quirky small games, like Journey where you surf the desert, that studio (named t**hatgamecompany**) will 100% shut down by next year unless they start telling more compelling stories with celebrities inserted into it licensed, and licensed songs, and good solid story telling and directing. You can't just be a quirky vibey game anymore. You need a hook, aka a influencer made it or actually make it good.

replies.author: sunnystormy64
replies.body:
So, let's take a step back. I'm going to go over some computer hardware pedagogy to help lay this out:

1. Each Mac mini is potentially its own pipeline, depending upon the amount of RAM each one has available.

2. Running a $400 / month Claude setup over two Mac minis implies that you have orthogonal work that can be performed. "Orthogonal" meaning no direct overlap.

3. A Mac mini with 32 GB of RAM would be equivalent to having 24 GB of VRAM (because of MacOS memory usage), so there are many local models you could run through ComfyUI. Furthermore, there are Qwen 3.8 27B fine-tunes that have cloud-model-level intelligence which you could local-host to orchestrate multiple pipelines.

4. Putting this all together: you'd have 10 local AI pipelines where you can get things done, and you'd technically only need one Claude subscription to orchestrate a server (could be a cheap machine) of interconnected Mac minis.

5. Or you use an 11th machine (Mac mini or equivalent) to local-host your orchestrator, pay no subs, and the only up-front cost is the hardware.

So, in summary: you may not need a Claude sub to solve your problem. Can you describe what tasks Claude is helping with to see if there's a local solution for it?

replies.author: Olmeca_Gold
replies.body:
Agents work autonomously within the scope I provide. So the system is not building everything at once. 

Say I decide to focus on biome houses and build them. It takes a 5-6 effective hours (where my pure attention is on them) to generate art style alternatives, choose one, pay attention to the process of building them etc. In reality it takes maybe two weeks to fully build 260 houses with interiors. But in parallel a lot of other work is done.

Say you need 50 factions, 400 creatures, 16 races etc. I have a narrative agent to create these as I go. So wordbuilding happens as I go.

Its also a DnD MMO so there is the entire rulebook onto which my agents easily base the mechanics.

I did spend 2 weeks to create a 500 page design document, onto which core features of the game mapped. But it was also AI assisted creation.

comments.author: yukajii
comments.body:
Game development differs wildly in different genres and niches. AA or AAA is still far from being realistic with team of just a few. 

No doubt solo devs released awesome projects, Stardew Valley being the best example. But most recent solo AI devs are making what are essentially prototypes, or vertical slices/demos at best. To make and maintain a successful game still takes a lot of resources and dedicated teams. Top casual mobile games still have teams of thousands of professionals.

But your specialization, i.e. marketing, is more and more important, since while building a product is in fact cheaper than ever, the distribution and user acquisition are crazy hard and expensive.
